Pairing with metals to build salts
plainLanguageExplanation: The halogens are Group 17 of the periodic table — the second-to-last column — and they are the most reactive family of nonmetals. Their members are fluorine, chlorine, bromine, iodine, and astatine. The secret of the family is electron arithmetic: every halogen atom has seven valence electrons, just one short of a full shell of eight. One short electron is a powerful craving. A halogen atom will grab an extra electron from almost anything that has one, which makes the pure halogens extremely reactive — chlorine is a greenish, dangerous gas, and fluorine is the most reactive element known. When a halogen grabs that one extra electron, it becomes a negative ion with a -1 charge, like chloride (Cl⁻). And here is the beautiful part: halogens pair perfectly with the alkali metals, because those metals have exactly one electron they want to give away. Sodium gives its one electron to chlorine, and the two lock into table salt, sodium chloride. Fluorine and chlorine also join carbon to build the plastics and everyday chemistry of modern life.

whyItMatters: The halogens are everywhere in your world. Chlorine keeps swimming pools safe and makes PVC plastic; iodine is essential for your thyroid; fluorine strengthens teeth in toothpaste; and sodium chloride — made from a halogen and an alkali metal — is the salt on your table. Understanding the halogens makes the seven-valence-electron pattern of the periodic table concrete and useful.
didYouKnow: The salt on your dinner table is a chemical marriage between two famous families — sodium, an alkali metal with one extra electron, and chlorine, a halogen that is one electron short.
compareReason: Seven electrons wanting one versus one electron wanting to leave — comparing halogens with alkali metals shows why the two families complete each other in compounds like salt.
